stemBlocks.value: In the diagram (not drawn to scale) R, S and T lie on a straight line with S between R and T. ST = 6 m, WR = 11.2 m, WT = 14.8 m and angle WRS = 90°. Giving answers to 1 decimal place, calculate (ii) the length RS and (iii) the measure of angle RTW.
Think first: The right angle at R makes WRT a right-angled triangle with WT as its hypotenuse, so Pythagoras gives the whole base RT before you strip off the 6 m.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p277-q12 from workbook page 277.

solutionSteps.instruction: Apply Pythagoras in right-angled triangle WRT, where WT is the hypotenuse.
Subtract ST from RT, since S lies between R and T.
In triangle WRT, identify WR as opposite angle RTW and WT as the hypotenuse.

strategyBlocks.value: Use Pythagoras in triangle WRT to find RT, subtract ST to get RS, then use the sine ratio (opposite WR over hypotenuse WT) to find angle RTW.

whyThisWorks.value: Because angle WRS is 90° and R, S, T are collinear, angle WRT is also 90°, so the whole triangle WRT is right-angled with WT as hypotenuse. That lets Pythagoras give the full base RT in one step, and RS is simply what is left of that base after the 6 m section ST. The angle at T then follows from the sine ratio, which needs only the side opposite the angle and the hypotenuse — both already known.

commonErrors.misconception: Adding the squares instead of subtracting; WT is the hypotenuse, so its square is the largest.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Adding the squares instead of subtracting; WT is the hypotenuse, so its square is the largest.

commonErrors.misconception: Finding RT and quoting it as RS without removing the 6 m.
